edbDesc: Fluorescence is a luminescence that is mostly found as an optical phenomenon in cold bodies, in which the molecular absorption of a photon triggers the emission of a photon with a longer (less energetic) wavelength. The energy difference between the absorbed and emitted photons ends up as molecular rotations, vibrations or heat. Sometimes the absorbed photon is in the ultraviolet range, and the emitted light is in the visible range.
title: Fluorescence
description: Some materials soak up invisible ultraviolet light and instantly give it back as visible colour, so they seem to glow under a black light. George Stokes worked it out in 1852 with quinine water, and named it after the mineral fluorite. It lights fluorescent tubes, makes highlighter ink and whitened laundry glow, and lets biologists tag cells with glowing proteins.
effect: a material absorbs light of one colour and instantly gives off light of a longer, redder colour
usedIn: Highlighter pens and optical brighteners in laundry detergent
Fluorescence microscopy with green fluorescent protein
strength: The glow lasts only billionths of a second after the light goes off; a fluorescent tube gives about four times the light per watt of a filament bulb.
pickWhy: Specific effect with many uses; the deck mentions fluorescence only in passing (electricity in a vacuum) and has no card for it.
